title: Hyperparameter Search
shortDefinition: The process of systematically finding the best model configuration through grid, random, or Bayesian optimization strategies.
definition: Hyperparameter search is the process of systematically finding the best hyperparameter configuration for a machine learning model — evaluating multiple configurations and selecting the one that produces the best validated performance — distinct from simply guessing good values based on defaults or experience. While experienced practitioners can often narrow the reasonable search space considerably, the interaction effects between multiple hyperparameters make fully manual configuration reliably suboptimal compared to systematic search in most cases.

sections.title: Three search strategies: grid, random, and Bayesian
sections.description: Grid, random, and Bayesian optimization offer different tradeoffs between thoroughness and efficiency.

content.text: Grid search exhaustively evaluates every combination of specified hyperparameter values — thorough but computationally expensive, scaling poorly as the number of hyperparameters and values per parameter grows (10 values for each of 4 hyperparameters = 10,000 combinations). Random search samples random configurations from the specified ranges — surprisingly effective, since random sampling covers the full space roughly uniformly and often finds good configurations faster than grid search at the same compute budget; empirically competitive with grid search for most practical purposes. Bayesian optimization uses the results of previously evaluated configurations to intelligently direct the next configurations to try — more efficient than random search for expensive-to-evaluate configurations, since it avoids wasting evaluations on regions of the search space that prior results suggest are unlikely to be optimal.

Grid search is appropriate when the search space is small (few hyperparameters, few values each) and exhaustive coverage is desired. Random search is a strong default for moderate search spaces — more efficient than grid search at equivalent compute budget, easier to implement than Bayesian optimization. Bayesian optimization justifies its added complexity specifically when each configuration evaluation is expensive (long training runs) and minimizing total evaluations matters most — the intelligence of Bayesian search pays off most when you genuinely can't afford many evaluations.

items: Grid search — small search spaces, exhaustive coverage needed.
Random search — moderate search spaces, good default choice.
Bayesian optimization — expensive evaluations, limited compute budget.
Tradeoff awareness — choose based on evaluation cost and search space size.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of hyperparameter search

content.text: Hyperparameter search has limitations. It can be computationally expensive, especially with grid search. The search can overfit to the validation data if not properly validated. Search results may not generalize to production data if the validation data is not representative. The search space must be defined well — too narrow misses the optimum; too wide wastes compute. Bayesian optimization requires careful implementation and can be complex. The best configuration found is only as good as the evaluation metric used.

items: Computational cost — can be expensive, especially grid search.
Validation overfitting — risk if not properly validated.
Generalization risk — results may not transfer to production.
Search space definition — too narrow or too wide both have issues.
Implementation complexity — Bayesian optimization requires care.
Metric dependency — search is only as good as the evaluation metric.

content.title: Important
content.text: Hyperparameter search is powerful but computationally expensive. Balance search thoroughness with compute budget and validate results on a held-out test set.

Running effective hyperparameter search requires careful strategy selection, validation, and budget management. The following practices can help ensure your search delivers improved model performance without excessive compute cost.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Define a reasonable search space based on domain knowledge.
Use random search as a default for moderate search spaces.
Use Bayesian optimization for expensive evaluations.
Evaluate configurations with cross-validation, not a single split.
Hold out a separate test set for final performance validation.
Set a compute budget before starting the search.
Document search space, strategy, and results.
Re-run search when data or model architecture changes significantly.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure performance improvement over default configurations — the value of hyperparameter search is demonstrated by how much better the optimized model performs than a reasonable baseline.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about hyperparameter search

items.question: What's the difference between hyperparameter search and AutoML?
items.answer: Hyperparameter search optimizes configuration values for a chosen model architecture; AutoML additionally searches over model architectures themselves. Hyperparameter search is a component within AutoML, but can also be applied independently to a fixed architecture.

items.question: How many configurations does a typical hyperparameter search evaluate?
items.answer: This varies by search strategy and compute budget — random and Bayesian search can find good configurations with 50–200 evaluations in many practical settings, while grid search might require thousands for the same hyperparameter space.

items.question: How do you avoid selecting hyperparameters that were lucky on the validation set?
items.answer: ClickMasters evaluates configurations with cross-validation rather than a single validation split, and holds out a separate test set specifically for final performance evaluation — never using the test set during search.

items.question: Is Bayesian optimization always better than random search?
items.answer: For expensive-to-evaluate configurations (long training runs), yes — the efficiency of Bayesian search justifies its complexity. For fast-to-evaluate configurations, random search is often comparably effective with less implementation overhead.

items.question: How long does hyperparameter search take?
items.answer: 4–14 weeks depending on training cost per configuration and search space size.

items.question: Can hyperparameter search be re-run when data changes significantly?
items.answer: Yes, particularly if new data substantially changes the model's optimal configuration — ClickMasters recommends periodic retuning when data distribution shifts are significant enough to potentially invalidate previously optimal configurations.

items.question: What is the difference between grid search and random search?
items.answer: Grid search tests every combination of specified hyperparameter values exhaustively. Random search samples configurations randomly from the specified ranges. Random search is often more efficient for moderate search spaces and finds good configurations faster with the same compute budget.

items.question: What is Optuna and how does it relate to hyperparameter search?
items.answer: Optuna is an open-source hyperparameter optimization framework that implements Bayesian optimization and other search strategies. ClickMasters uses Optuna as the primary tool for hyperparameter search due to its efficiency and ease of use.

items.question: Can hyperparameter search be parallelized?
items.answer: Yes — grid search and random search are trivially parallelizable since each configuration is independent. Bayesian optimization is more difficult to parallelize but can be done with asynchronous sampling strategies.

items.question: What is the role of cross-validation in hyperparameter search?
items.answer: Cross-validation provides more reliable performance estimates for each configuration than a single validation split. It reduces the chance of selecting hyperparameters that perform well on one particular data split by chance.
